Deploy per `.edgepoint/standard/deploy.md`. Scope: (whatever the builder typed after the command name) if given.

## Before you deploy

Run `edgepoint check`. If acceptance tests fail, stop and tell them what's broken.
Do not ship red tests because the builder asked you to ship — tell them what would
go live broken, and let them decide with that in front of them.

Run `edgepoint checkpoint "before going live"`.

Check for open escalations. If something was never built, say so now rather than
letting them discover it in production.

## Business questions that only arise at ship time

Real decisions, asked once, following `protocol/questions.md`:

- **Is this going live for real customers, or somewhere private to look at first?**
  Ask every time until they tell you to stop.
- **Real data or test data?** Especially payments and emails — sending live email
  from a test run is the classic first accident.
- **Anything that shouldn't be visible yet?**

## The things that become true the moment it's public

Say these **once**, at the first real launch, and never again unless something
changes. They are not questions and not blockers — they are three obligations
that attach to the builder the day customers can reach the site, and they will
not hear about them from anyone else until someone is annoyed with them.

Keep it to a few sentences. A wall of legal text at the moment someone is excited
to go live is how it gets skipped entirely.

**If the app collects anything about a person** — every webapp does:

> Going live makes you responsible for your customers' personal data under the
> Data Privacy Act. Three practical things: name someone as your Data Protection
> Officer, which for a business your size can be you; if data ever leaks you have
> **72 hours** to tell the National Privacy Commission and the people affected,
> so tell me the moment you suspect it; and there's a short report to file once a
> year even if nothing happens. Registering with the Commission is only required
> above 250 staff or 1,000 people's sensitive records — worth knowing where the
> line is.

Check before you say it: the privacy notice exists, is linked from every form,
and says what the app actually does. If it doesn't, that is a build task, not a
launch conversation.

**If they sell to the public**, one more:

> Online sellers have to show their real business name, address and contact
> details on the site — not just a contact form. Tell me what to put and I'll add
> it now.

**If anything on the site looks like a receipt**, confirm it says what it is:

> What your customers get after paying is an order confirmation, not a BIR
> invoice — you keep issuing those the way you do now. If you'd rather the system
> issued the official ones, that's a conversation with your accountant first, and
> I'll explain why when you want it.

Then stop. Do not enumerate penalties, do not quote section numbers, and do not
turn this into a compliance review. If they ask a question you cannot answer,
say plainly that it's one for their accountant or a lawyer, and note it in
`escalations.md`.

## Deploying

Push to `main`. GitHub Actions builds the image and the server pulls it. That is
the whole deployment — do not run builds on the server, do not `docker build`
locally to ship, and do not invent a deploy script. See `standard/deploy.md`.

Watch the run. If it fails, read why and say so in one sentence.

Don't ask about hosting, the server, TLS, or the pipeline — all settled. Secrets
are the exception: ask for exactly the ones you need, one at a time, say what each
is for and where to get it, and never write one into a file that gets committed.

### The first deploy is different

If the server has never been set up, this is not a normal deploy. It needs a
Lightsail instance, `deploy/provision.sh`, DNS, and repository secrets — the
checklist is in `standard/deploy.md`. Walk the builder through it, one step at a
time, or tell them plainly it needs a developer for an hour. Do not attempt it
silently.

### Migrations

The deploy applies them and takes a backup first. Say plainly, before shipping
anything that drops or renames a column, that rolling back the code will not roll
back the data.

## After

Tell them:

- the URL, and whether it's public
- what to click first to confirm it's really working
- anything switched off or stubbed
- **how to undo it** — going back is one command and takes seconds, because the
  previous version is still on the server. Every non-developer's first question
  about going live is whether it can be taken back down, whether or not they ask.

No deployment logs. No build output. If it failed, one sentence about what failed
and what you're doing about it.
